Why ownership can exceed 100%Finviz (and similar sites) add up shares reported on quarterly 13F filings and divide by shares outstanding. Figures above 100% are a known reporting artifact, not a physical impossibility. Common causes:Short selling / stock lending: Institution A owns shares and lends them. Institution B borrows and sells short. Institution C buys those shares. Both A and C can report owning the same shares. 
Timing mismatches between filings, share-count changes (buybacks, issuance), and occasional double-counting (e.g., a fund and a fund-of-funds).  
 
investopedia.com 
 
 
When you see ~104%, actual institutional ownership is already very high. It often also implies meaningful short interest. Treat the exact percentage as “extremely high professional ownership,” not a precise ownership census.What “Institutional Transactions 31.33” meansFinviz defines this as the percent change in total institutional ownership. A reading of +31.33 means the reported institutional ownership percentage rose by that amount versus the prior reporting snapshot (driven by latest 13F data).  
 
finviz.com 
 
Positive = net buying (existing holders adding shares and/or new institutions appearing). 
It is not “number of institutions.” You can have fewer funds owning more shares, or many small new positions. 
Data is lagged. 13Fs are filed up to 45 days after quarter-end, so the picture is already weeks to months old. 
Finviz does not publish a crystal-clear “exactly last 6 months vs last quarter” note on every quote page the way some tooltips do for insider transactions. In practice this field tracks the latest available 13F-to-13F change. Two quarters of data would cover roughly six months, but the number you see is the latest reported change, not a guaranteed all-time record. 
 
So: institutions were net buyers in the latest disclosed period. That is not the same as “more institutions than ever in history.” To check breadth (how many distinct funds) and multi-year history you need the holders list and historical 13F tables, not just this one Finviz field.What institutional buying actually signalsInstitutions are mutual funds, ETFs/index funds, pension funds, insurance companies, hedge funds, banks, endowments, and RIAs that manage other people’s money and generally must file 13Fs once they have $100M+ in relevant U.S. equities.Net buying can mean:Active managers did research and decided the stock is attractive at recent prices. 
Passive/index funds bought because the stock is in an index or a benchmark they track (little stock-specific “conviction”). 
Existing large holders simply added. 
 
 
Liquidity and “respectability”: high institutional ownership usually means better analyst coverage and easier trading for large size. 
 
It does not guarantee the stock will go up. Crowded high-ownership names can be volatile if funds later sell together. The lag means they may already have finished buying (or started selling) before you see the number.How “confident” are they, and what researchers do they have?Confidence is mixed and uneven:Active funds (stock-pickers, some hedge funds) typically have equity analysts, sector specialists, portfolio managers, and often quantitative/risk teams. They model earnings, competitive position, valuation, and catalysts. A large new or increased active position is a stronger signal than an index fund adding. 
Passive funds (Vanguard, BlackRock iShares-style products, many pensions) buy because of index rules or asset-allocation policy. Their “research” is mostly benchmark construction, not a deep bullish thesis on that one company. 
Hedge funds range from deep fundamental research to short-term trading and quant models. 
 
A +31% jump in the ownership percentage is a sizable flow, so someone with professional staff increased exposure. You cannot tell from Finviz alone whether that is high-conviction active buying or mechanical index buying. Look at the actual top holders and whether they are active or passive, and whether holder count rose, not just the percentage.Bottom line: 103.93% ownership = institutions (plus short-related double-counting) dominate the share register. +31.33 transactions = they were net buyers in the latest 13F window. That is useful context—“smart money” and index money have been accumulating—but it is lagged, imperfect, and not a substitute for looking at who the buyers are, short interest, float, and the company’s fundamentals.

There is no controversy regard ISR.  People had them but less 1% discontinued in the clinical trial due to ISR.   
 
Yes, the data from Nektar’s own Phase 2b trials (REZOLVE-AD in atopic dermatitis and REZOLVE-AA in alopecia areata) support what you heard: injection site reactions (ISRs) are common but almost never lead to patients stopping treatment.  
 
ir.nektar.com 
 
In the 16-week induction period of REZOLVE-AD:ISRs occurred in about 70% of rezpeg-treated patients (vs ~4% on placebo). 
99.6% were mild or moderate. 
Discontinuations due to ISR were under 1% (specifically reported as 0.6%). 
Most were self-resolving.  
 
ir.nektar.com 
 
Later 52-week data showed a similar picture: discontinuation due to ISR around 0.7%, with ISRs becoming less frequent during maintenance dosing (every 4 or 12 weeks). In the alopecia trial, Nektar reported zero discontinuations due to ISR.  
 
ir.nektar.com 
 
In short: high incidence of (mostly mild) ISRs is real and has been a talking point, especially from Lilly and some analysts. But the claim that patients are frequently stopping treatment because of them is not supported by the Phase 2b data Nektar has presented. The disagreement is more about how commercially relevant the reactions will be than about the discontinuation numbers themselves.
